title: When a Parent Refuses to Move: How Families Actually Get Through the Conversation
description: Practical ways Memphis families handle a parent who refuses assisted living: how to start the conversation, what to say, who to bring in, and what to do if they are unsafe.
meta_title: When a Parent Refuses to Move to Assisted Living
meta_description: Practical ways families handle a parent who refuses assisted living: how to start the talk, what to say, who to involve, and what to do if they are unsafe.
main_html:
Quick answer

Most parents who refuse to move are not refusing care. They are refusing to lose their home, their independence and their say. The approaches that work give your parent real choices, start small with a visit or a short stay, bring in people your parent trusts such as their doctor or pastor, and take several short conversations rather than one big one. If your parent has the capacity to decide, the decision is theirs, and your job is to make the safest option the most appealing one. If they no longer have capacity and are unsafe, a power of attorney or, as a last resort, the courts are how decisions get made.

A refusal to move is a parent's decision, or reaction, against leaving home for assisted living or memory care even when family believe it is no longer safe to stay. It usually reflects fear of losing control and independence, and is handled through repeated conversations, trial stays and trusted voices, unless the parent lacks capacity.

This guide is practical, not clinical. It reflects what Memphis-area families and community staff say works, and what usually makes things worse.

Why parents say no

  • Losing control. Every other decision is being made for them: doctors, driving, money. This is the one they can still make.
  • Losing home. The house holds a marriage, children and decades of memory. Leaving it can feel like the end.
  • Fear of a "home". Many parents picture the nursing homes of decades ago. Modern assisted living looks very different, but they have not seen it.
  • Not seeing the problem. Dementia can take away the ability to recognise one's own decline. Your parent may truly believe they are fine.
  • Money worries. Fear of spending what was meant for the children, or of running out.
  • Pride. Not wanting to be a burden, or to look like they need help.

Knowing which of these is driving the refusal changes what you say. Ask, and listen to the answer.

Which path are you on?

  1. Your parent can understand the risks and the choices, and is reasonably safe for now: work on the conversation over weeks, use trials and visits, and add help at home meanwhile.
  2. Your parent can understand the choices, but is unsafe now: be direct about the specific risks, bring in their doctor, and offer a respite stay as a short-term step.
  3. Your parent can no longer understand the risks because of dementia: involve their doctor, act under a power of attorney if one exists, and focus on a calm move rather than winning an argument.
  4. There is no power of attorney and your parent lacks capacity and is in danger: speak to an elder law attorney about conservatorship, and contact Adult Protective Services if there is immediate risk.

How to start the conversation

  • Start early, before a crisis. The best conversations happen months before a move is urgent. After a fall or a hospital stay, choices shrink.
  • Talk about them, not the plan. "What worries you most about living here?" works better than "We think you should move."
  • Name specific events. "You fell twice in the bathroom last month, and you were on the floor for an hour" is harder to dismiss than "you're not safe".
  • Use "I" statements. "I lie awake worried about you" invites a response; "You can't manage" invites a fight.
  • Keep it short. Plant the idea, then stop. Come back to it in a week.
  • Pick the right person. Sometimes it is the child your parent listens to; sometimes it is not a child at all.

Give real choices

A parent who feels the decision has been made for them will resist. A parent choosing between options is deciding, not being decided for.

  • Shortlist two or three communities that fit and let your parent choose between them.
  • Let them choose the apartment, the furniture to take, the timing.
  • Offer the choice of "more help at home now, and we look again in three months" if it is genuinely safe.
  • Avoid false choices. "Do you want to move to A or B?" only works if "neither" is not a safety disaster; be honest about what is negotiable.

Our guide on how to choose a care home helps you build a shortlist your parent can choose from.

Start small: visits, meals and respite

  • A lunch, not a tour. Invite your parent to lunch at a community, or to an event. Many Memphis communities host open activities and holiday events.
  • A friend who lives there. Nothing changes a parent's mind like a friend from church or the old neighbourhood who is happy there. Ask around.
  • A respite stay. Many communities offer short furnished stays, often a week or a month. Present it as a break while the house is repaired, after a hospital stay, or while a carer is away. Many respite stays become permanent because the parent likes it.
  • Adult day programmes. A few days a week of company and activity can make the idea of a community less frightening.

Bring in voices your parent trusts

  • Their doctor. Ask the doctor, before the appointment, to talk about safety at home. Many parents accept from a physician what they will not accept from a child.
  • Their pastor or faith leader. In Memphis, church is often where trust lives.
  • A geriatric care manager or social worker: a neutral professional who has had this conversation many times.
  • Community staff. Experienced admissions staff are good at this. Let them talk with your parent directly.
  • Siblings, together. Agree among yourselves first. A parent will find the gap between children who disagree.

Address the money fear directly

Parents often refuse because they think it will cost everything they have saved for the family. Show them the numbers. Put the cost of staying at home with the help they actually need, including home care, repairs, meals and transport, next to the cost of assisted living. Sometimes the gap is smaller than they think. Our guides to what assisted living costs and how families pay help with the comparison.

What usually makes it worse

  • A surprise family meeting with the decision already made.
  • Arguing about memory with a parent who has dementia. You will not win, and it frightens them.
  • Threats, ultimatums and "for your own good".
  • Touring the most expensive, largest community first when your parent would prefer something small.
  • Selling the house before your parent has settled.
  • Lying about the move entirely. Gentle framing is different from deception that destroys trust.

When your parent cannot decide safely

An adult with capacity has the right to make decisions others think are unwise, including staying at home. Capacity is about whether your parent can understand the information, weigh the risks and communicate a choice. Their doctor can assess it.

When dementia has taken that capacity away:

  • Durable power of attorney for health care: if your parent signed one while they had capacity, the agent can make care decisions in line with your parent's wishes and best interests. Find the document now.
  • No power of attorney: Tennessee law provides for a court-appointed conservator for a person who is disabled and cannot manage their affairs. It is a court process with costs and time; speak to an elder law attorney.
  • Immediate danger: if your parent is at serious risk of harm, contact Adult Protective Services, and in an emergency call 911.

Even with legal authority, the move goes better when it is calm and kind. Community staff can help plan the day.

If they agree: making the move stick

  • Move familiar furniture and set up the apartment before your parent arrives.
  • Visit often in the first weeks, or follow staff advice if your parent settles better with a short gap.
  • Expect a hard few weeks. Many parents ask to go home at first and settle within one to three months.
  • Keep promises you made: visits, outings, church.
  • Do not sell the house the week after the move if you promised it would wait.

Questions that open the conversation

  • What worries you most about living here on your own?
  • What would make you feel safe and still in charge?
  • If something happened at night, what would you want to happen?
  • Would you come to lunch at one place with me, just to see?
  • Would you try a short stay while we fix the bathroom?
  • Would you talk to Dr. [name] about it with me?

When siblings disagree

Many families find the hardest conversation is not with the parent but between siblings. One lives nearby and sees the daily decline; another lives away and hears a parent say everything is fine. Before you talk to your parent, talk to each other. Share the specific events, the doctor's view and the money picture. Agree who will lead the conversation and what each of you will say if your parent asks. A neutral professional such as a geriatric care manager can help a divided family agree a plan.

Making home safer while you talk

If the conversation will take time, reduce the risks at home meanwhile: grab bars and a shower chair, a medical alert pendant, a pill dispenser with alarms, removing loose rugs, meals delivered, a home care aide for the hardest parts of the day, and someone checking in daily. These steps buy time and also show your parent what help looks like, which can make assisted living feel less of a leap.

Words that tend to help, and words that do not

Small changes in wording change how a parent hears the idea.

  • "Community" or "apartment" rather than "home" or "facility".
  • "Help with the things that have become hard" rather than "care".
  • "Try it for a month" rather than "move".
  • "You decide between these" rather than "we have decided".
  • "I need to know you are safe so I can sleep" rather than "you can't cope".

None of this is about tricking your parent. It is about describing what assisted living actually is, in terms that do not set off the fear of the nursing homes of fifty years ago.

faq.q: What do I do if my parent refuses assisted living?
faq.a: Find out what the refusal is about, usually loss of control, home or independence. Then give real choices, start small with a lunch visit or respite stay, bring in people your parent trusts such as their doctor, and talk in several short conversations.

faq.q: Can I force my parent to move into assisted living?
faq.a: Not if they have the capacity to decide; an adult with capacity can make choices others think unwise. If dementia has taken that capacity, a health care power of attorney or a court-appointed conservator can make decisions.

A short furnished stay at an assisted living community, often a week to a month. Many families use it as a trial, and many respite stays turn into a permanent move once the parent sees what it is like.

faq.q: How do I talk to a parent with dementia about moving?
faq.a: Keep it simple and calm, avoid arguing about memory, focus on comfort and safety, and do not hold long debates. Let the doctor and experienced community staff help plan the move.

faq.q: Who can help persuade my parent?
faq.a: Their doctor, their pastor, a geriatric care manager or social worker, a friend who already lives in a community, and experienced admissions staff. Agree among siblings first.

faq.q: What if my parent is in danger and still refuses?
faq.a: If your parent lacks capacity, act under a health care power of attorney or speak to an elder law attorney about conservatorship. If there is immediate risk of serious harm, contact Adult Protective Services, or call 911 in an emergency.

faq.q: How long does it take a parent to settle after moving?
faq.a: Many parents ask to go home in the first weeks and settle within one to three months. Familiar furniture, regular visits and keeping promises help.

faq.q: Should we sell the house right away?
faq.a: Not if you promised your parent it would wait, and not before they have settled. If money is tight, renting it or a short-term bridge loan can buy time.
